title: Stronger Adjectives: When "Very" Is Not Enough
dek: Learn 50 stronger adjectives, how they differ in meaning and strength, and when very is still the best choice.

blocks.text: *Very good* and *very tired* are correct, natural English, and often the best choice in speech. A stronger adjective is useful when it says something more **specific** than "very + adjective". This guide shows 50 options, explains how they differ, and shows when to keep *very*.
blocks.say: Very good and very tired are correct, natural English, and often the best choice in speech. A stronger adjective is useful when it says something more specific than "very + adjective". This guide shows 50 options, explains how they differ, and shows when to keep very.

blocks.text: Rule 1: some adjectives do not take "very"
blocks.say: Rule 1: some adjectives do not take "very"

blocks.text: Adjectives such as *good, big* and *tired* are **gradable**: they have degrees, so *very good*, *quite big* and *a bit tired* all work. Strong adjectives such as *excellent, enormous, exhausted* and *terrifying* already mean "extremely", so we do not normally say *very excellent* or *very exhausted*. With these we use *absolutely*, *completely* or *really*: *absolutely exhausted*, *completely wrong*.
blocks.say: Adjectives such as good, big and tired are gradable: they have degrees, so very good, quite big and a bit tired all work. Strong adjectives such as excellent, enormous, exhausted and terrifying already mean "extremely", so we do not normally say very excellent or very exhausted. With these we use absolutely, completely or really: absolutely exhausted, completely wrong.

rows: The food was very good. / The food was absolutely excellent.
It is a very big house. / It is an absolutely enormous house.
I am very tired. / I am absolutely exhausted.
I am very hungry. / I am absolutely starving.
It is very cold. / It is absolutely freezing.
blocks.caption: Gradable and extreme adjectives
blocks.say: Gradable and extreme adjectives. For example: good means excellent. big means enormous. See the full table on the page.

blocks.text: Rule 2: strong words change the meaning, not just the volume
blocks.say: Rule 2: strong words change the meaning, not just the volume

blocks.text: *Very sad* and *devastated* are not the same. *Devastated* suggests a shock or a serious loss. *Very small* and *microscopic* are not the same either: *microscopic* means almost too small to see. Before you replace *very + adjective*, check that the new word still says what you mean, and check its register (informal, neutral or formal).

Five scales to know

blocks.text: Each table moves from a neutral word to stronger ones. The examples show typical partners. Strength is a guide, not a measurement: native speakers disagree about exact order.

a brilliant idea; flawless English; exquisite craftsmanship
blocks.caption: Scale 1: good
blocks.say: Scale 1: good. For example: Neutral means good, nice, fine. Stronger means great, impressive, excellent. See the full table on the page.

rows: a disastrous failure (it describes the consequences)
blocks.caption: Scale 2: bad
blocks.say: Scale 2: bad. For example: Neutral means bad, poor. Mild means disappointing, inadequate. See the full table on the page.

blocks.caption: Scale 3: big
blocks.say: Scale 3: big. For example: Neutral means big, large. Stronger means huge, enormous, massive. See the full table on the page.

blocks.say: Scale 4: beautiful and interesting. For example: Looks (neutral to strong) means attractive, gorgeous, stunning, breathtaking. Interest (neutral to strong) means engaging, fascinating, captivating, enthralling. See the full table on the page.

I am worn out after the trip.

outraged (angry at something unfair), seething (very angry but quiet)

blocks.say: Scale 5: tired and angry. For example: Tired: neutral means tired. Tired: mild to strong means weary (literary), drained (no energy), exhausted, worn out. See the full table on the page.
50 options, grouped by meaning

blocks.text: Read the notes. Many of these words are *not* simply "stronger": they add a meaning or a register.
blocks.say: Read the notes. Many of these words are not simply "stronger": they add a meaning or a register.
Feelings and sensations

rows: *Miserable* is unhappy in general; *heartbroken* follows a loss; *devastated* means a strong shock.
*Delighted* is common and polite; *ecstatic* is extreme.
*Stunned* means shocked and silent for a moment.
*Exhilarated* means excited and full of energy.
*Anxious* is stronger and lasts longer; *concerned* is milder and polite.
blocks.caption: Feelings and sensations
blocks.say: Feelings and sensations. For example: very sad means miserable, heartbroken, devastated. very happy means delighted, thrilled, ecstatic. See the full table on the page.
Quality and value

rows: Very strong. Use for things, not people.
*Tedious* is boring and long; *monotonous* never changes.
*Straightforward* means simple to do or understand.
*Challenging* sounds positive; *arduous* is tiring and long.
blocks.caption: Quality and value
blocks.say: Quality and value. For example: very good means excellent, outstanding, superb. very bad means awful, terrible, dreadful. See the full table on the page.
Size, speed and degree

rows: *Miniature* is a small copy; *microscopic* is almost invisible.
*Sluggish* is negative; *leisurely* is relaxed and pleasant.
Both describe a very strong sound.
*Dazzling* means too bright to look at.
*Deserted* means no people where you expect them; *vacant* means not in use.
blocks.caption: Size, speed and degree
blocks.say: Size, speed and degree. For example: very big means enormous, gigantic, massive. very small means tiny, miniature, microscopic. See the full table on the page.
Temperature and condition

rows: *Ancient* for history, *elderly* for polite talk about people, *outdated* for ideas.
*Penniless* means with no money at all.
*Overpriced* means more than it is worth.
Neither is "stronger". They sound more positive, because *cheap* can suggest low quality.
blocks.caption: Temperature and condition
blocks.say: Temperature and condition. For example: very cold means freezing, icy. very hot means boiling, scorching. See the full table on the page.
People

rows: *Frail* is physically weak, often older people.
*Idle* means not working; *lethargic* means without energy.
blocks.caption: People
blocks.say: People. For example: very smart means brilliant, intelligent. very brave means courageous, fearless. See the full table on the page.

blocks.quote: **A note on "very depressed":** *Depressed* is a clinical term. Unless you mean a medical condition, words such as *down*, *miserable* or *despondent* are often more accurate in everyday conversation.
blocks.say: A note on "very depressed": Depressed is a clinical term. Unless you mean a medical condition, words such as down, miserable or despondent are often more accurate in everyday conversation.
When "very" is the right choice

items: *It was a very good film, but not a masterpiece.* *Very good* shows a high but not extreme level.
*That's very kind of you.* *Very* is natural and polite here. *Compassionate* would sound odd.
*I'm very sorry.* This is a fixed polite phrase.
blocks.say: It was a very good film, but not a masterpiece. Very good shows a high but not extreme level. That's very kind of you. Very is natural and polite here. Compassionate would sound odd. I'm very sorry. This is a fixed polite phrase.

blocks.text: Use a stronger adjective when it is more exact, not to sound more advanced.
blocks.say: Use a stronger adjective when it is more exact, not to sound more advanced.

blocks.explanation: *Excellent* is an extreme adjective, so use *absolutely*, not *very*.

Summary

blocks.text: Keep *very* for everyday speech and polite phrases. Choose a stronger adjective when it is more exact, and use *absolutely* or *completely* with extreme adjectives. Always check the meaning, not just the strength.
blocks.say: Keep very for everyday speech and polite phrases. Choose a stronger adjective when it is more exact, and use absolutely or completely with extreme adjectives. Always check the meaning, not just the strength.
